text:
JayZ, thank you so much for this amazing channel for us noobs. You got it right... many of us are first time builders but with extra time at home these days. 
I have a Request/Challenge for you.  With my limited knowledge as a newbi it seems that BOTH the 6900 Ryzens vs. Nvidia 3080 series are all but unavailable.  But I need something now as I am building a system around MS FS 2020 and X Plane (as a professional flight instructor/flight school).

Task: I am working on  a build for MS FS 2020 and I want to build something that is easily upgradable.  I.e. I would like to do a build with a good mother board, good RAM and other basic features, but I want to use a 1080 (or comparable) initially and then in a few months from now when 3080 series or Ryzen series or better are more readily available with kinks worked out, replace my card and ramp up my MS and X Plane settings. 
So my primary concern is being able to do the "build" and swap out the Graphics card later.  

The second issue I have is that I am expecting for VR to soon be available on MS and other simulators, and I know I will be connecting at least 3 screens and lots of PERIPHERALS (Yoke, consoles, throttle quadrants, Radio interfaces) that use lots of USB drives these days.  Even some of the smaller moving map displays use USBs. 
So my focus initially isn't on graphics because the dirty secret among us flight instructors is, that we don't care about graphics as much since we use this to teach INSTRUMENTS- but functionality - thats important.  To that end I don't mind spending an extra couple hundred bucks on a MB (it seems like the different between a crappy MB and one that runs various USB C and has lots of capability is only a few hundred bucks at most so correct me if I am wrong, but this is where the investment should be) if it gives me lots of expandability. 
Would you recommend a MB GC then that is Intel / Nvidia oriented?  

What would you recommend and how would you "Plan for functionality now and upgradability later"?  

Anyhow, I like and appreciate your channel and that you explain not just the what and how, but the "Why" so I would love to hear your thoughts.

text:
AMD are always behind the curve with the drivers. They start with profiles for their launch games and then back fill the other titles. They get there eventually and I suspect they will this time. Maybe not the card you want to choose if you are an early adopter. I definitely take on board the point on older games, I have a few that I play and these will be lowest on the list to get fixed in the drivers. So might be a consideration if you run lots of older games. I know in the past some of my MMORPG buddies that bought AMD had terrible experiences that never really got rectified, there is only so far back worth optimizing. The running hot is also typical AMD, it does cause more crashes, especially in a hot ambient temps, but they do seem prepared to push harder than Nvidia out of the box. Nvidia leave more headroom usually, but if you aren't the overclocking type it is irrelevant other than that slight extra stability.

Still I think it is what you would expect. We know they don't have the same budget as Nvidia, so there has to be sacrifices. Maybe if they gain enough market share this time around they will be better financed to solve these problems in the future. Recommending not to buy it seems moot, when you can't buy anything. text:
@trilight3597  I'm using a 5700 XT right now with the latest drivers and no issues at all. And I game everyday. And this isn't my first AMD card. I'm sure some of the criticisms are valid, but IMO, a vast majority are unfounded and stems from hearsay and ignorance. It's easy to jump on the bandwagon and make unsubstantiated claims. Yes, AMD has had driver issues and may still have some bugs, but the overexaggerated claims being made by many with little to no experience and others with an agenda, are laughable. 

And I'm by no means an AMD fanboy considering I've been supporting Nvidia from the day 1(when 3dfx was their competition). My last Nvidia card was an RTX 2070 that died and had to repaired under warranty.  So my experience hasn't been so rosy. After this happened to me for no reason I can think of, I did some research and discovered lots of similar complaints regarding the RTX 2000 series. Some involved driver issues and others, dead cards. So, Nvidia is not immune to problems. They just get a pass because they're more popular.

I absolutely agree they have more features and pretty much own the content creation market. And sure, If I was into content creation and /or streaming, I'd probably have a 3080 or 3090. But content creators make up a small portion of the gaming market. 

My problem with large youtubers like Jay is they are often sponsored by large companies who can easily influence their reviews. l saw it plain as day with Jay. If you're testing 2 enthusiast cards, show the best of both cards. That's what some of the smaller youtubers do and the reason why many prefer to watch them. The more thorough the benchmarks are, the better the information quality. But, apparently, it's easier to be lazy and form an opinion on flimsy facts, than take the time to do a good job. Especially when you'll get thousands of views anyway.

text:
AMD is not showing it's "greed side" by not support SAM on Ryzen 3000 and earlier, the hardware just does not support it - it requires specific support in the PCIe root complex in the CPU.   Intel has included support for resizable BAR (aka SAM) since Haswell but it requires a UEFI update to enable it.

"(T)he PCI-Express root complex of Ryzen 5000 "Vermeer" processors introduce an instruction called full-rate _pdep_u32/64, which is required for resizable-BAR to work."

text:
Jay wins the worst, most inaccurate RDNA 2 review, with added bonus on not knowing how IPC works. Was this award won by just luck alone, or was there hard work behind it, that's the question. Did you release the results with power limited card? Ghost recon wildlands was faster even with 6800XT than 3080 on 4K, even though AMD is much faster at 1440p and 1080p. Was these results poor because of 1440p or 1080p? Both having exactly 100fps suggest some hard limit, for whatever reason, as there's zero change that you could optimize game so poorly that it wins 15% on 4K but loses 30% on 1440p, especially when 1440p is much stronger for RDNA2.

6900XT is the fastest 1440p gaming card on the planet. And with 16GB it will stay that way vs. the competition at least this console generation. 1440p with highest textures on 100% nextgen console games will require more than 10GB, as consoles have 12/14GB and can stream assets much faster with low latency, so games will have huge variance of textures eventually. On PC with longer draw distances, more/better effects and techniques, and with some buffer because you can't stream assets the same way, that 16GB becomes necessary much faster than people realize. Or 10GB won't be enough would be the better way to put it.

I would certainly not buy 6900XT, as 6800XT is way better in value. But better silicon with more headroom for overclocking and the above reasoning, it's certainly worth it to some. And for those who are willing to pay whatever to get the fastest 1080p card for some competitive edge, it might be worth it. Lets hope for a miracle that AMD releases bios that allows Infinity Cache overclocking, and manual latency tuning. That way you could get much more from these cards, especially from the best binned silicon 6900XTs.

text: OK, we need to talk about driver optimization for games. Yes, AMD has historically been worse at it than Nvidia. However, the real problem here is neither Nvidia nor AMD, but the game companies. If they were doing everything right, none of these optimizations would even be necessary. You know what these optimizations are? Band aids for the game devs screwing up. This is a slightly extreme example, but in one case, the game just completely failed to make the video end of frame call. This is part of why the driver packages are the size that they are now, hundreds of individual game fixes to address devs breaking standard protocols. And, unfortunately, we have normalized this behavior on both the consumer and development sides of the fence. (For the record I work at a major game development and publishing house, and we are just as guilty of it as everybody else.)

text:
@gerhardsmith7892  against other cards in games, the intended use case. By testing real games you get real data, in aggregate it becomes more than specifc titles by testing enough games. Also when you see a specific game benchmark it's easy to relate to and think "oh that's a framerate I would be satisfied with in this game at x resolution at y settings with these visuals."

The synthetic benchmarks are attempting to be a stand in for real games by trying to mimick the relative performance scaling across many GPUs. How much they succeed is debatable. I have no objection to then in general. The issue is that having 5 of them is an extremely high proportion.
author: @Arjun-eb1yc

text:
@Arjun-eb1yc  
On that I agree, but in your original comment it seemed like your problem was with synthetic benchmarks as a whole, but now that you clarify I agree with you
author: @gerhardsmith7892

text: @Arjun-eb1yc  Those benchmarks measure different things. They aren't all equivalent, so having 5 is not just a matter of more tests is more accurate. They are not a stand-ins for real games. They are control tests for various portions of the graphics technology. Measuring games is not controlled tests. There's too many variables. The difference is empirical versus statistical analysis.

text: @Jayztwocents you spoke of SAM and how Ryzen 3 CPU's should already support this on the same motherboards. But if AMD picked up SAM recently (which they did, but of course couldve done before, but intel didnt either) they did not prepate the ryzen 3000 Series CPU's for SAM. It's a protocol which needs native-instructions inside the processor to work properly. If they're not installed in the cpu, the cores would need to emulate this using microcode which will slow SAM down by quite a devastating amount. Thats why I wouldnt call out AMD for not supporting it earlier, instead I'm giving them props for being the first to finally implement the protocol into their cpu's.

text:
Good video as always Jay, however there is information out there as to why AMD have not and probably will not enable SAM for the 3000 series CPU's, and it is not pure greed.

"TechPowerUp notes that the new Ryzen 5000 CPUs are the only AMD series to integrate the PCIe physical layer feature called full-rate _pdep_u32/64, which allows processors to see the GPU’s entire video memory as a single addressable block instead of separate 256 MB apertures. It is true that Zen2 CPUs use the same IO die and PCIe controller as Zen3, but AMD SAM is actually controlled through a new ISA CPU instruction set. These specific instructions are only emulated in microcode using other similar instructions in the Zen2 and older cores, and this makes everything predating the new Ryzen 5000 essentially too slow to benefit from the performance uplift offered by SAM. "

It's worth noting that this is a feature that has been baked into Intel cpu's since (I believe) the 4000 series.

So jay telling that is amd's greed is just an uninformed comment, and jay being a "techtubber" should totally be informed. BTW intel has it since haswell at hardware level, that's why they can implement it.

author: @Gooch8181

text:
No, it's nothing more than cheating right now.  "Smart Access Memory" is NOT some kind of magical thing that AMD invented for the 6000-series cards.  "Smart Access Memory" is actually more related to PCIe slots.  By default, PCIe slots limit the amount of memory that can be accessed on a GPU.  "Smart Access Memory" simply increases that amount, which provides a performance boost of up to maybe 15% in a few games and makes no difference whatsoever in others.  

Posting those numbers would do nothing but artificially inflate the performance of these cards in comparison to Nvidia cards RIGHT NOW (which is seemingly what all of these pathetic AMD fangirls are looking for...they DESPERATELY want the 6900XT to out-perform the 3090...BUT IT DOESN'T!) because Nvidia will ALSO be enabling "Smart Access Memory" on their 30-series GPUs with a driver update in the near future.  And unlike AMD, who tried to FORCE gamers to buy a new X570 mobo, a new Zen 3 CPU AND a new 6000-series GPU by making "Smart Access Memory" ONLY USABLE when a 6000-series GPU is paired with a Zen 3 CPU on a X570 motherboard, Nvidia's version of "Smart Access Memory" will work on ALL of their 30-series GPUs with ANY CPU and ANY motherboard from Intel OR AMD...their version will even work on PCIe 3 mobos.

That is why I said it would be "cheating" to post those numbers now...because "Smart Access Memory" IS NOT a feature that is EXCLUSIVE to AMD GPUs.  So when Nvidia releases their drivers to enable "Smart Access Memory" on their cards, that is going to increase the performance numbers of the 3060, 3070, 3080 and 3090 cards too.  Why would it be acceptable to post the "SAM" results right now when Nvidia cards are getting the exact same feature in the next few weeks?  That is something that only an AMD shill would do, which is why certain channels ARE actually doing that right now.  Once it is available on the Nvidia cards THEN you can show the results for both AMD and Nvidia GPUs.

From what I can understand, you go to custom, leave pretty much everything default, then turn on free sync optimised, v-sync set to on unless specified in game  (opinion differs, I also use it with Riva tuner), leave triple buffering off, turn surface optimisation off, leave pretty much everything off and do so in game as well. Try different combos until it works and update your display port cable to a vesa certified one. Also, freesync on/optimised. Freesync/vsync on, correct hertz etc.

text:
About the 250 vs 300 watt power.
AMD wattman looks at GPU power only. The 300 watt is for the Total card. So including memory and VRM losses.
So i think AMD's setting is correct. But since the voltage is still quite high its still power limited.

When running stock power target lowering the Target voltage can help making the boost curve more aggressive  (higher clocks with less voltage)  and because of that increate performance within the same power.
I thought a 6800 had a max power of +- 200/210 watt shown in Wattman when you have stock power.

You can do a bios readout with the MorePowerTool and then you will see 203 watt GPU power for the 6800 and the 6800XT will show 255watt.

text:
Interesting observations.  Every setup is different of course, but other reviewers didn't seem to have these problems.  HWUB has the most games tested in their review, while GN has the most detail.  In the HWUB final average, the 6900xt beats the 3090 in 1440p (and 1080p), but loses in 4k, by a pretty small margin in either direction.  Given the price difference, the 3090 only makes sense if you highly value RTX as it's currently implemented in current games, or if you do professional work, otherwise the 6900xt is a better value.  The story is similar for the 6800xt and 6800.  Apart from RTX/DLSS/Professional use cases, they're generally faster than nVidia cards in most normal (rasterized) gaming, with nVidia closing the gap or slightly winning in 4k.  Unless you have a 120hz+ 4k  tv or monitor,  anyone on a display that only does 60hz in 4k, this is irrelevant.  I would never run at 60hz.  My TV, like most good TV's pre-HDMI 2.1, can do 120hz at up to 1440p, thus until I get a new TV, I will always and only game at 1440p with maxed out settings and AA, which looks more than sharp enough anyway.  Here the AMD cards win, period, the end.  Again, unless you're really all about that rtx/dlss in the relatively few scenarios where it applies. 

And make no mistake, going forward, due to the consoles, as well as improving drivers, the AMD cards WILL fare better in ray tracing in the future - not saying they'll overtake 3000 series, but they will do much better than what the "old" rtx titles show, which were programmed for nVidia RTX... the newer open source microsoft dx12 ultimate ray tracing - anything made for the ps5/series x, WILL perform well on AMD cards by design... these will handily outperform the consoles which always offer a "good' experience by design.  This will be because of 2 factors: more favorable programming to the AMD hardware, and more specified (less extensive perhaps?) use of raytracing effects.  Instead of being wasteful and tanking framerates for a negligible fidelity increase, the RT effects will be used more wisely to offer a visual enhancement where it matters without tanking performance.  Future AMD DLSS equivalent is supposedly on the horizon too although we don't know how it will compare.

text:
On the subject of pricing, the price to go off of is really more the price board partners are typically saying the cards should be retailing at.

Yes that may involve actually looking across competing partner cards and coming up with your own result from that. Hopefully in the future board partners will more be the companies announcing prices over chip providers who as this generation has shown will gladly have their marketing teams push one singular figure out over and over when the only entity operating on that price is themselves. Presumably either offering their own cards at a loss and so with limited very controlled offerings or with very narrow mark-ups that a 3rd party partner can't realistically operate on with their additional costs factored in.

Good example of this is the RTX 3080. A card Nvidia say retails from £650 in the UK and advertise the FE as £650 from them directly, but seem very keen to ensure isn't stocked all that frequently. Now board partners have their own opinion on this and retail the card from the floor price point of £740, with most retailing for a range closer to £800-£840. That's not scalping mark-ups, not ramping up prices to exploit demand.... that's just the price seemingly every board partner out there making 3080's has decided is the cheapest price they can offer a RTX 3080 and still actually see some kind of return. Once stock balances out, unless Nvidia have already pushed out a 3080 ti/super variant and partners are then looking to just empty out base 3080 variant stock... £740 is the floor price you'll get a RTX 3080 for unless Nvidia suddenly have a explosion of FE stock to offer, which I can't see happening as I suspect Nvidia are making significant less on the FE then they'd like and the idea of it being a option is more there just to give their marketing teams pricing message some actual substance.

Now if people talking about the 3080 started referring to it as the "£740 offering" which is what pretty much all of their viewers will actually be paying at the absolute minimum even in a ideal world where stock is abundant, then suddenly the actual content of the discussion changes and comparisons change signfiicantly.

text:
The reason why 1kW psu are good is not that the actual power usage is 1kW, but efficiency, power spikes and temperature. Basicaly all psu are most efficient when the output is ca. 30-80% of max power. The closer to 100%, the worse. + this extra efficiency means less heat, meaning less noise AND more efficiency.
If gpu suddenly pulls more power, than average, it could overload the psu or trigger protection, making your system unstable if you don't have headroom. So yeah, extra power is good.
And even if PCs actually start using 1kW, this would be only in case with heavy loads. Most of the time power usage is well bellow of max.

RDNA2 arch does have the better ipc here.

higher clock speed doesn't mean the design itself has worse IPC.

both 3090 and 6900xt are great cards, they perform well via different approaches.

3090 = relatively slow clock speeds, massive fp32 core count
6900xt = high clock speeds, half the fp32 core count.

text:
Jay you realize Nvidia does the same thing with clock boosting right. They advertise their clock rates on the spec sheet then out of the box their cards run faster than the listed spec's show on the spec sheet and everybody praises them for that.

AMD on the other hand has most always listed their actual clock speeds and the cards adhere to that except this generation on RDNA2 where these new cards behave more Nvidia like and run past their listed speeds and some have said oh they are running past their listed speeds or oh they don't over clock well.

Well if you got a card listed as 2250MHz and it runs out of the box at 2350MHz-2500MHz it is already overclocking itself past the listed spec speed and if it stays within the llisted power usage or at least close to it I see no problem with this. If the card runs at 2400-2500MHz out of the box stock and you OC it to 2600-2700MHz that to me is a huge OC for something like a GPU since in the past we have never seen those kind of over clocks on any kind of GPU including Nvidia and if you did it was by using exotic cooling such as LN2 and not on air cooling ever.

As for IPC I disagree if you look at how Nvidia lists their cores now where they list them as double from how they used to in the past and then you look at AMD using the 6900XT as an example with 5120 stream Cores and then you have the 3090 listed as having 10496 Cuda cores. According to Nvidia they have just over double the GPU cores and yet AMD is able to match or beat the 3090 in most things important excluding RT. So by Nvidia's own way of listing cores now AMD has a huge upper hand for IPC and Nvidia did that to themselves by listing double the Cuda cores because they made some internal changes to the Ampere GPU's.

As for power at 250 watts pretty sure that is a driver bug the card is listed as 300 watts so it should have been pulling at least up to 300 watts out of the box. AMD needs to work on their drivers and also make sure reviewers get fully working drivers so crap like this does not come through in reviews and everything works as it should. Hell HW Unboxed said the 6900XT was a poor over clocker because he could not go past 2700MHz. When I heard that I was like WTF bad over clocker dude if you are getting anything past 2300MHz as an OC on a GPU that would be considered a huge OC since GPU's are so much more complex than a CPU & getting up to 2600-2700MHz on a GPU on air was unheard of on any GPU before AMD released RDNA2 cards. I guess we get spoiled very fast these days.

Edited:
I was not trying to be rude or make your review sound like I was not liking it. I thought it was decent and about what I expected from the over priced 6900XT card. That is match or come close to the 3090 for 500-600USD less than the 3090 card. I would like to mention though if a 3070 even beats the 6800XT or 6900XT cards even in one game test there is something very wrong with the review drivers & AMD needs to take a look at any game that has the lowly 3070 beating the 6800-6900 cards. As for RT to me at least it is a waste of time and not worth the performance hit for what it offers in return. Now AMD does need something like DLSS 2.0 for sure yes it is a cheater for performance but it seems like that is the way the industry is heading is finding way to cheat to get more performance and if it does not impact the appearance of the render output then it is a cheat I can live with and use.

text:
IIRC, AMD said that while SAM could in theory be supported by Zen 2, it would severely hurt performance. Because on Win10 it relies on the PDEP instruction. Which is technically supported by Zen 2, but only in microcode, not natively in-silicon as is the case with Zen 3.

While certainly not a perfect analogy, its difference in speed and efficiency is a bit like software encoding and decoding of H.265 (HVEC) video, vs native hardware accelerated encoding and decoding. If you have a beefy enough CPU, you could do it by software, but it'll bog down your CPU hard and be slow work. Not exactly conducive to being a performance improvement feature.

text:
Not all optimizations can be made in drivers, some things simply needs to be fixed or updated on the game/software end. Especially when old games, meet new hardware architectures, that come to the point where it's time to trim away some of the increasingly "heavy anchors" of in-silicon legacy hardware compatability layers, as is the case with RDNA2 (and Zen 3).

Ampere didn't see these things hit quite as hard, because it's basically a half-step iteration of Touring, which game developers had 2 years to work on before Ampere came along. RDNA2 is significantly more of a new thoroughbred architecture, vs RDNA "1" which was a halfway new one with maaassive in-silicon legacy compatability layers back to GCN. RDNA2 as we know it, has only been widely available to devs for a few months at this point. Some games, like those 4+ year old ones that don't have a top 10 active player base, aren't brand sponsored titles, and aren't such old superclassics as to basically have their whole engine baked into the GPU driver package (exaggeration ofc but only a little) - those often take ages to get patched for new architectures. Or never get actually get patched for that, they just ride along on those legacy hardware compatability layers.

I fully expect RDNA2 to age very well, but first mature well, because as it is at the heart off both new primary consoles, game and game engine devs will learn to use its strenghts, and hide it optimize for its weaknesses, very well. It won't transfer directly, but it should help compensate substantially, for less attention given due to lower market share.

author: @miket7217

text:
@miket7217  Please reconsider your language, there's no grounds for being rude here. 

Zen 2 is compliant, but PDEP instruction is only supported through microcode. Zen 3 has instruction support natively in-silicon. Microcode only instruction easily costs 100+ cycles vs in-silicon 1.

Could SAM be enabled with Zen 2? Sure, absolutely. But it would absolutely and horrendously tank performance. Not improve it. Not exactly conducive to "performance enhancment features".

Overly simplified, we're basically, principally talking similar performance differences of software based video decoding/encoding, vs native in-silicon ("hardware accellerated") decoding/encoding.

If you're absolutely gonna insist on pointing fingers, I'd rather suggest you point it at Intel. They have had native in-silicon support for this for 7 and a half years before AMD did, ever since Haswell.

In reality though - these instructions  and resulting feature had no real use in the consumer or enthusiast hsrdware space until these last few months, when some PCIE4.0 enabled high end GPUs could actually leverage it for a minor avantage. They only came in to Intel desktop and HEDT line around Haswell, as tagalongs with stuff like VT-d and other bare-metal virtualization features - most of which 99.98% of desktop consumers and enthusiasts have never used, nor even been aware of their existance. They've lain there in the bundle, dormant and irrelevant for almost a decade.

text:
Jay... really, get your numbers right or just inform yourself how the power readings on those cards actually work.

You are mixing AMDs and NVidias Power Numbers butr you shouldn't because they are measured differently.

First of all, let's get the TOTAL BOARD POWER Numbers right: For AMD it's TDP, the TGP is only total graphics power (Chip + Memory but no VRMs etc.)
RX6800 - 250W
RX6800XT - 300W
RX6900XT - 300W
RTX3070 - 220W
RTX3080 - 320W
RTX3090 - 350W

NVidia measures the Power for the limits at the PCIe Slot + PCIe Power from PSU. So therefore, NVidia shows everything the whole card sucks up on the sensor and therefore applies the limits to the whole card.

AMD only measures GPU & Memory and shows this on sensor, therefore, it is cut off at around 250 Watts, because the VRM and other stuff on the board takes up energy as well and another 50 Watts seem plausible for that. If you would measure the power on the cables + PCIe Slot (via riser) you would measure quite exactly 300W powerdraw for both, 6800XT and 6900XT. When you set the +15% Power the core + Memory itself cam suck up to 300W which means the total board power exceeds the 300W. But since everything you are able to do is looking at sensor numbers in software, you confuse two totally different sensor values and ways to measure and regulate the power draw of the cards between NVidia and AMD.

Sorry, I like the entertainment on this channel, but your technical knowlegde about the stuff you want to review is at least incomplete sometimes.

Jay, I like the video, but its the driver and you know that.  Here's why.  Let's go back to the launch of 5000 series gpu's.   AMD came out with the 5600, which was a good card.  What happened?  I'll tell you what happened.  Nvidia being the scum they are dropped the price of the 2060ti down to 5600 level pricing and they were still competitive while NVidia was losing money. AMD unveiled the 5700 series.  What happened?  NVidia dropped the pricing on the 2070.  AMD unveiled the 5700xt.  What happened?  NVidia dropped the price of the standard 2080 non-TI.  So yeah, its a driver issue.  Lisa Sue knows that NVidia has another switch to be flipped because NO "T.I. or Super" cards have been announced yet.  The driver will come we all know that, they are stopping NVidia from being the monster of controlling the market pricing.  

You mentioned SMART Access Memory.  You bet your ass they are gonna leverage it.  There isn't a company on the planet that wouldn't.  NVidia has ALWAYS favored Intel processors so it sort of levels the playing field. So sitting at 3070 numbers right now IS NOT A BAD THING.  If people are gonna go out and get the "New Hotness" in AMD processors,  why would they not get the GPU to match and get the most use out of that processor.  My turn to use a car reference.   Thats like buying a brand new Corvette to turn around and put Dusan All Season Tires on it and drive in the snow.  Would you do that?  No, of course not.  So I say its OK where its at because the battle is gonna be waged at the higher price point cards.  WE ALL KNOW that AMD is gonna flip the switch and turn that sumbitch up with a driver update when NVidia announces the new TI or Super models for their 3000 series GPU's.  

Add 10 fps here for smart access memory, add 200 to 300 mhz with larger cache available to use with rage mode there and a couple of other hidden chipset features and its gonna be a 3080 killer for sure.  The hardest part about launches is you won't see the final results until both manufacturers have all their chips on the table.  This is the preliminary challenge until the main event.

text:
Jay, I have a slight problem with your methodology in testing the GPUs. You specifically say “We don’t turn on DLSS or Rage Mode because that’s not how they come out of the box, and most people just run them like that.” 

While you might be right when talking about ALL users, I’d be willing to bet that most of YOUR viewers don’t run them as they come out of the box. Or, if they do, it’s because they don’t know that clicking a single button in the management program will gain them 10%+. In which case you should show what the GPUs do with those modes enabled, so perhaps those people will say, “Hey, maybe I should turn this thing on!”

Yes, it might be “unfair” to run an Nvidia card with DLSS enabled against an AMD card that has no DLSS option. But, to NOT turn DLSS on is like trying to compare a car with a turbo 4-cyl engine to one that doesn’t have the turbo, then disabling the turbo on the first car to make them “equal”. No – run the cards against each other with all their bells and whistles enabled and see which one wins. 

Obviously, there has to be a line somewhere. I think that drawing the line and excluding Smart Access Memory (until Nvidia comes out with their equivalent, at least) is fine – it requires a significant hardware purchase. Also, overclocking is out, because a) most people (even your viewers) won’t really do that, and b) it shouldn’t affect FPS that much.

TLDR – don’t compare these cards “as they come out of the box” – compare them “as they will be used in your PC”.

text:
I think it's time for YouTube PC hardware reviewers to start seriously grappling with the impact of software feature enhancements on card performance. Continuing to run AMD against NVIDIA in benchmarks with DLSS off is getting to the point of almost feeling misleading. The landscape has changed - the raw capability of the hardware is no longer the deciding factor in performance differences. The story right now shouldn't be that AMD has achieved performance parity, because they haven't - NVIDIA with DLSS on is way out in front. The real story right now is that software performance boosters are now nearly as important as the hardware they are running on. The only way to get out of this is if someone can present a compelling reason to run most of the time with DLSS off, or if turning on Rage Mode and Smart Access Memory actually makes up a significant amount of the DLSS gap.

I understand that this complicates doing reviews, and makes them more time consuming. But at this point, the information presented here really isn't useful in making a buying decision. It probably gives some nice validation for the design engineers at AMD but in the info presented here doesn't really describe the experience I would actually have if I bought one of the cards in the benchmarks.

text: That's Basically the premise of Ampere, vs recent former gens. But just like HT, it's not exactly "double the cores" / performance. Each 2nd unit in and Ampere SM can do either integrer or floating point, instead of one dedicated for each. So they can so FP(32)+FP(32) per cycle, not just FP(32 or 64)+INT as previous gens. But they still can't do INT+INT / two Integer operations at once, which is why the "double the CUDA count" stuff is BS. So yeah, tve performance increase is more akin to HyperThreading. Really beneficial if those extra "threads" are doing the right type of calculation, but nowhere near what actual double the actual cores could do. Nvidia basically took away the FP64 capability from the SMs ("CUDAs") of non datacenter GPUs, and replaced it with FP32 and ability to do 2x FP32 operations per cycle (but not 2x INT).

text:
@comagnum1  the only reason his review has it framed in a bad light is due to poor software side of things. 

I'm someone that really enjoys CPU overclocking. I made sure my system could handle the extra power draw cleanly, and had the cooling to give me as much headroom as I can get. That is to say I'm one to push my system. But I don't really even bother with GPU overclocking, maybe I'll tune the fan curve but that's usually it. When people like me don't even bother to try and get extra performance from cards the out of box performance matters, and AMD completely dropped the ball here. 

Even if it was running at those specs out of the box, my whole thing is that it's in a much different spot. They can kind of get away with comparing it to the 3090, but that cards known to be crap value for gaming. On the workstation side of things the extra memory and Nvidia features in a lot of professional software makes it a pretty good deal. 

I went into this already thinking the 6900XT would be the king for gaming at a price that could be decently argued over, and the only thing that kept me from leaving with that same feeling is software that held back the card which is very much a fair light to shine on it. If you think he put it in a bad light I think you might just want it to be as good as you imagine, and I hope they fix things and get it there, but reality is it's not there now.
